gene_editing.abstract: Quantitative Biology > Genomics arXiv:2611.08853 (q-bio) [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026] Title: Synchronized Optimal Transport Reconstructs Coupled Transcriptomic and Chromatin Dynamics Authors: Jingfeng Wang , Yanxiang Zhao , Qing Nie , Zixuan Cang View a PDF of the paper titled Synchronized Optimal Transport Reconstructs Coupled Transcriptomic and Chromatin Dynamics, by Jingfeng Wang and Yanxiang Zhao and Qing Nie and Zixuan Cang View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Single-cell RNA and ATAC data collected across developmental stages provide time-course snapshots of transcriptional and regulatory states. Since sequencing is destructive, trajectories between these snapshots must be inferred from independently sampled cell populations. Existing approaches typically infer continuous dynamics in a single modality or integrate RNA and ATAC in a shared representation. Here we present Cross-Omics Aligned Trajectory Inference (COATI), which extends unbalanced synchronized dynamical optimal transport to time-dependent cross-modal maps for reconstructing coupled trajectories in distinct RNA and ATAC state spaces. We evaluated COATI on synthetic benchmarks and four developmental datasets using held-out-stage reconstruction and lineage analyses. COATI improved reconstruction of cell populations at held-out stages, including recovery of chromatin-state heterogeneity within cell types, and better preserved developmental lineage relationships. The unbalanced formulation allows the inference of population mass changes, which were shown to associate with DNA-replication programs at early stages and lineage-maturation programs later in development. The coupled trajectories enabled analysis of lineage-specific transcriptional and chromatin changes and their temporal relationships during development. Lineage responses inferred by COATI agreed with independent CRISPR perturbation results, and the inferred regulatory patterns were consistent with independent epigenetic data. Abstract RNA predates cells, but today it “lives” inside them. Most current RNA is short-lived, folded, and often edited from its chromosomal origins, but it governs its own phenotypes. Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup, serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA–DNA–PROTEIN network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation, we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction–survival (R/S) axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these has contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where “RNA did not lose” in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy, and in its various forms, it has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.
